blocks.text: So good afternoon. Today we are going to share some early and ongoing work from the AI and Data Infrastructure Learning Lab. In fall 2025, when we began this work, Pennsylvania was experiencing a rapid influx of proposed AI data centers, over 50 active or planned projects statewide. While data centers themselves are not new, the recent surge is driven by AI's demand for always-on, high-capacity computation. These facilities require enormous amounts of electricity, water, land, and they place new strains on regional energy systems. Yet many communities reported learning about these developments only after land purchases had already occurred or construction planning was underway. In the fall and summer of 2025, we began to hear more and more about data center negotiations in communities, and our PI, Dr. Ray, began developments in Memphis, Tennessee, and noticing a pattern between what was happening there and what was happening across the country. And Pennsylvania is a unique state with rural, urban, and suburban areas that are all being impacted by proposed AI data center developments. And it was challenging to get a sense then where this was happening as there was a lack of centralized monitoring. So while there are now a few different projects that are tracking data center proposals across the U.S., in fall 2025, we got in contact with Amelia Doda, who is the software developer behind the website formerly called PA Data Center Proposals. Now it's called trackdatacenters.com with more of a national focus. Amelia is actually from northeastern PA and was following her community's response to multiple proposed data center developments. She began mapping similar negotiations across PA, initially mapping these out to see if there were any patterns in the locations and sites of industrial extraction, such as coal mining. Last time we spoke, she was connected with other software developers and groups interested in expanding the data set for a more open source nationwide focus. And this is outside of her actual day job. Just wanting to put a face behind this website and highlight how these mobilizations and community engagement are individuals who are choosing to spend time and labor on this meaningful work and are shifting and it's changing over time and leveraging different networks and media. This was something that we are interested in in this study. Yes, there are a lot of these data center proposals, but what's happening with all the news about rising community backlash. In Pennsylvania specifically, data centers must navigate municipal zoning processes. Zoning is a legislative framework delegated by the Commonwealth that determines how land can be used. Importantly, if a proposed data center complies with existing zoning, there may be limited opportunities for direct public oversight. However, Pennsylvania's Sunshine Act requires that official deliberations and decisions occur in public meetings with notice and opportunity for public comment. These municipal meetings thus become a critical site where communities attempt to intervene, contest, and make sense of development decisions. So here is our conceptual framework for this initial work that we are doing. Much media and policy discourse frames community engagement as nimbyism or not in my backyard. We find this framing limiting because it presumes narrow self-interest and obscures the complex sense-making work residents are actually doing. In our case, residents were not saying not in my backyard, but rather not here and not anywhere without accountability or even questioning the broader development model itself. From a learning sciences perspective, this framing erases the labor of learning, relating, and reasoning that communities undertake over time. Instead, we conceptualize public comments in municipal meetings as speech apps that operate within governance. These comments create public records, function as moments of collective knowledge-making, and support coalition building. In our view of AI data centers as place-based infrastructures, we view these as having physical, social, environmental, and political consequences. And so, for example, as I mentioned earlier, experts' testimony is valued differently from the community members as a social category. And that has an impact on how decisions are made. So that is an example of a political consequence. So speakers language in use constitutes and instantiates public record making. And a second conceptual framework is that public comments are forms of knowledge making and coalition building. So before Giselle shares more about the methods, I am just going to share our research question here. And it's what topics of concern do municipal meeting public commenters raise to their city council regarding AI and data centers

blocks.speaker: SPEAKER_01
blocks.text: In terms of limitation of our project, our positionality as outsiders to the setting is one of the primary limitations. Also, as the source of the data is recorded live stream videos of municipal meetings, they are not empirically validated descriptions of data center impacts, but rather narrative accounts that reveal how community members interpret, contest, and attribute meaning to AI infrastructure in their local context. Moving forward, we expand our analysis to examine how concerns are discursively framed with particular attention to how languages in use construct coalitions, as illustrated in the following example. I don't have any children, but I care about your kids, and I'm not willing to sign them up to be a real-time experiment of how much poison air you can breathe. I hope that you guys aren't willing to do that either. In addition, we take into account Pennsylvania's role within the national energy system to understand how AI infrastructure intersects with regional energy systems. This includes its role as an energy exporter, the historical and current significance of liquefied natural gas and nuclear energy, and the ways in which large load interconnections place stress on a system with an already long queue dominated by renewable energy projects. Lastly, we aim to conduct participatory, community-engaged research to better align our work with residents' priorities. We will reflect on the question of what does it mean to create partnerships with community members while navigating historically uneven ways that university-based partnerships can dominate community spaces. We will care about processes of partnering to enable collective transformative agency. Lastly, as a conclusion, our work intends to support sustainable community futures with the present AI technology. So we assert here today, AI infrastructures are not abstract, neutral, or despatialized like the word cloud. Rather, they're physically, socially, effectively tied to space and are politically consequential. Thank you so much.
